newsitem.title: USA: Army general subpoenaed in border killing case.
newsitem.headline: Army general subpoenaed in border killing case.

text.p: An Army general in charge of military forces used in the drugs war on the U.S.-Mexico border was subpoenaed on Tuesday in connection with last month's killing of a teenager by a U.S. Marine.

Military officials said Gen. James Lovelace was subpoenaed by the Texas Rangers law enforcement agency to appear before a grand jury or at least provide documents for the grand jury's investigation into the death of Esequiel Hernandez.
Hernandez, 18, was killed near the small border town of Redford on May 20.

Military officials said Hernandez was shot because he opened fire on a group of four Marines patrolling the area, but his family insisted he was tending his herd of goats at the time and only carried a .22-calibre rifle to scare away wild dogs.
Texas Rangers investigators said they have problems with the military's account of the incident, and want to know why the Marines did not immediately administer first aid.
"It is not a situation we would consider self defence," Texas Rangers Capt. Barry Caver told Reuters.
He said Hernandez either pointed the weapon or fired at the Marines from at least 700 feet away and then turned away and walked off in the opposite direction.
The Marines followed him for at least 20 minutes before one opened fired with an M-16 rifle from about 425 feet away, he said.
"It was a pretty dang good shot," Caver said, adding that Hernandez apparently lay bleeding for 22 minutes before the Border Patrol arrived and had ambulance attendants provide medical assistance.
An autopsy report showed that Hernandez bled to death.

Caver said Lovelace, who heads the Task Force Six military agency which backs up civilian forces in the drugs war, would be asked to provide information on the agency's policy on the use of force. A Task Force Six lieutenant colonel was also subpoenaed on Tuesday.
Caver said he expected a grand jury in Fort Stockton to examine the case in mid-July.
"We will present our facts to the grand jury and they will decide what, if any, charges there'll be," he said.
